extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, peer reviewers, and people interested in scholarly publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative dimensions used in the peer review of scholarly research and the practices journals/editors/reviewers follow to assess, select, and prepare manuscripts for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria: competence, significance, and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific peer review has been defined as the evaluation of research findings for competence, significance, and originality by qualified experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peers act as sentinels on the road of scientific discovery and publication; these three dimensions (competence, significance, originality) are the core attributes reviewers are asked to judge when evaluating research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity / Double-blind review
rubrics_metrics.description: The review process was double-blind to provide anonymity for both authors and reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-blind review is used to provide anonymity and reduce bias; cited studies suggest double-blind can affect representation (e.g., favour increased representation of female authors) and is a major axis of policy choice for journals weighing bias reduction against practicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of peer review (formatal dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of Peer Review (e.g., single-blind, double-blind, open, post-publication, multi-stage open peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different types (open peer review, double-blind, post-publication peer review, multi-stage open peer review) have distinct effects on reviewer behaviour, transparency, and editorial processes; journals choose models based on trade-offs among quality, speed, and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review / publishing peer review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review and publishing peer review reports (making referee reports visible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence cited on effects of open peer review (e.g., randomized trials, observational studies) shows publishing reports can alter referee behaviour and recommendations; transparency is promoted as a means to improve accountability and possibly review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered reports / preregistration and protocol review
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered reports: a publication model where protocols are peer-reviewed and accepted in principle before results are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registered reports are presented as a means to promote reproducibility and reduce publication bias (results-blind review), with several journals and fields adopting them; they involve protocol review and can decouple publication decisions from study outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data availability and archiving
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies to ensure that the underlying data for articles are made available to researchers now and in the future (e.g., AGU 'Policy on Referencing Data in and Archiving Data for AGU Publications', NSF Data Management & Sharing guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and professional bodies adopt data policies and archiving requirements to support reproducibility and data reuse; these policies can include mandatory data deposition, referencing datasets, and guidance on data management plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility as an evaluative aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review's relationship to reproducibility, and interventions to promote reproducible research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites concerns about reproducibility crises and references interventions (registered reports, protocol review, data policies) and literature assessing reproducibility; reproducibility is an explicit criterion and motivation for many reforms to peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducing publication and reporting bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms and policies to reduce publication bias and reporting bias (e.g., results-blind review, conclusion-blind review, two-step manuscript submissions, registered reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several proposals and pilot studies (results-free review, registered reports, two-step submissions) are discussed as means to reduce bias toward significant or novel results; editorial policy can be designed to mitigate these biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility and decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: What editors should do when referees disagree and the broader editorial role in ensuring quality, fairness, and integrity of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are cited as having a possible role in ensuring review quality, adjudicating referee disagreements, and maintaining fairness and integrity; guidance and studies discuss editorial practices for resolving conflicting recommendations and preserving standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal peer review (pre-submission/institutional review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal review can include content review, copyediting, evaluation of style and tone, as well as overall readability or fit for the journal's audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal peer review at institutions or within research groups is presented as a mechanism to improve manuscripts before journal submission, covering both substantive content and presentation/readability aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of financial conflicts of interest and industry payments by editors, authors, and reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites evidence of discordant disclosures and industry payments; transparent disclosure practices are framed as necessary to maintain trust and integrity in peer review and editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review quality metrics: acceptance rates, review times, and review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational metrics for journals including quality, acceptance rates, and review times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies and reports measuring journal operations (acceptance rates, times to decision, quality metrics) are used to evaluate the state of peer review and identify areas for improvement such as speed and efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection and nomination practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices around suggesting or excluding reviewers, journals allowing author-nominated reviewers, and risks (including fake reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that suggesting/excluding reviewers can influence publication outcomes and that some processes (e.g., author-nominated reviewers) have been abused (fake reviews). It implies guidance to be cautious about reviewer nomination and vetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review as gatekeeping for quality, fairness, and innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception of peer review as a gatekeeping function to control quality, fairness, and encourage innovation in published research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cited works debate peer review's effectiveness as gatekeeper; the rubric implied is that peer review should balance quality control, fairness, and openness to innovative or heterodox work while avoiding conformity or suppression of novel ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement of manuscript quality through peer review and editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review and editorial processes aim to improve manuscript quality (manuscript quality before and after peer review and editing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence cited (e.g., studies measuring manuscript quality pre/post review) positions peer review and editing as mechanisms for improving clarity, correctness, and overall presentation of research.
